title: An Architectural Review of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was the first novel-view synthesis method to deliver radiance-field image quality at real-time frame rates on consumer hardware. This reportreviews it as an architecture, tracing how each design decision follows from a single constraint: the scene representation must remain rasterisable at render time anddifferentiable during training. Neural radiance fields store a scene implicitly in network weights, so every pixel costs hundreds of network evaluations along a ray, keeping training at hours to days and rendering at seconds per frame; explicit grid structures reduce training to minutes but still march rays, while point-based splatting renders quickly without matching volumetric quality. 3DGS instead stores the scene as anisotropic 3D Gaussians carrying opacity and view-dependent spherical-harmonic colour.The report examines the four components that make this viable---the factorisation of the covariance into a rotation and a scale, which keeps it positive semi-definite underunconstrained gradient descent; the spherical-harmonic colour model, repurposed from irradiance environment maps; the EWA projection, whose local affine approximation preserves the Gaussian form through a non-linear perspective divide; and the tile-based rasteriser, whose single sort per frame serves both rendering and backpropagation---together with the adaptive density control that grows and prunes the primitive set in response to image error. On the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark the method reaches $27.21$~dB PSNR and $0.214$ LPIPS at $134$~fps, surpassing the previous quality leader in perceptual similarity while trailing marginally in PSNR and rendering roughly three orders of magnitude faster.
